covers: A take that concedes half the received wisdom — the format most likely to pull in a fabricated study for support.
idea: Argue that cardio does not kill your gains, but the way most lifters do cardio does: an hour of hard intervals the morning of a leg day is not the same thing as a walk. The problem is placement and intensity, not cardio itself.

hooks.text: Cardio is not killing your gains. Your timing is.
hooks.rationale: Contradicts the belief plainly while keeping the half that is true.

hooks.text: You can run and get stronger. Most people just do both badly.
hooks.rationale: The strongest true version of the idea, stated flat.

hooks.text: There's one thing that decides whether cardio costs you anything, and it isn't how much you do.
hooks.rationale: Opens the gap on placement without naming it.

hooks.text: You dropped cardio to protect your gains and now the stairs are a problem.
hooks.rationale: Names the frustration the viewer is actually living in.

hooks.text: An hour of hard intervals the morning of a leg day is not the same thing as a walk.
hooks.rationale: Leads with a concrete comparison the idea already contains.

sections.text: Cardio is not killing your gains. Your timing is.
The advice got flattened into avoid cardio, and a lot of people took it seriously.

An hour of hard intervals on the morning of a leg day will take something out of that leg day. A walk will not. Same word, two completely different demands. Put the hard stuff on a day you are not squatting, or after the lifting instead of before it, and most of the conflict disappears. The problem is placement and intensity, not cardio.
You get to keep your heart and your squat. It was never actually a choice.
Find your hardest cardio session this week and move it one day.

claims.text: The conflict comes from placement and intensity, not cardio.
